dotPoints.description: Distinction between nominal GDP and real GDP

prompts.question: Explain the distinction between nominal GDP and real GDP.
markerNotes: Reward the explanation that real GDP removes the effect of price changes, so growth reflects output rather than inflation
A worked example in which nominal GDP rises while real GDP is flat shows application of the concept
commonStudentErrors: Describing real GDP as the value of output at current prices
Confusing the price level with the quantity of output
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains clearly the distinction between nominal and real GDP, including the role of prices and the GDP deflator, with a worked example showing how the same output can produce different measures
5 marks: Explains the distinction with accurate reference to prices and at least one example
4 marks: Explains the distinction with accurate detail but without an example
3 marks: Describes nominal and real GDP with some accuracy
2 marks: Identifies nominal or real GDP
1 mark: Makes a general statement about GDP

sampleAnswers.answer: Nominal GDP measures the value of all final goods and services produced in an economy in a period, using current prices. Real GDP measures the same output using constant prices from a base year, so it removes the effect of price changes. The difference matters because nominal GDP can rise simply because prices rise, even if output does not change. For example, if output is unchanged but prices rise by 5 per cent, nominal GDP rises by 5 per cent while real GDP is unchanged. The GDP deflator, which is the ratio of nominal to real GDP, measures the price level and shows how much of any change in nominal GDP is due to inflation. Real GDP is therefore the appropriate measure for judging growth in output.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the distinction is explained through constant and current prices, the role of inflation is shown with a worked example, and the GDP deflator is identified.

sampleAnswers.answer: Nominal GDP uses current prices and real GDP uses constant prices from a base year.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 3-mark response states the distinction with some accuracy. Explaining why it matters and giving an example would move it up.

sampleAnswers.answer: Real GDP is more accurate than nominal GDP.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response makes a general statement without explaining the difference.

dotPoints.description: Limitations of GDP as a measurement, specifically the exclusion of population, hours worked, the informal economy, the non-market sector, distribution of income, environmental degradation and depletion of the resource base

prompts.question: Analyse the limitations of GDP as a measurement, including the exclusion of population, hours worked, the informal economy, the non-market sector, the distribution of income, environmental degradation and depletion of the resource base.
markerNotes: Strong answers show that GDP can rise while wellbeing falls, for example through environmental damage that is counted as production
Reward the distinction between what GDP measures and what it omits, such as unpaid household work
commonStudentErrors: Listing limitations without analysing how they affect the interpretation of growth
Claiming that GDP measures wellbeing directly
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained analysis of how the exclusions from GDP limit it as a measure of economic wellbeing, weighing the effect of each exclusion on the interpretation of growth and reaching a reasoned judgement on its usefulness
5-6 marks: Analyses at least three limitations with accurate evidence and a link to wellbeing
3-4 marks: Describes limitations of GDP with some accuracy
1-2 marks: Makes a basic or general statement about GDP

sampleAnswers.answer: GDP is a widely used measure of economic activity, but the limitations of GDP mean it is an incomplete guide to wellbeing. It excludes unpaid work, such as caring and household production, and the informal economy, so output that people value may not be counted. Population and hours worked are also not reflected, so GDP per person or per hour may give a misleading picture of living standards. The non-market sector, such as volunteering, is largely excluded, which understates the contribution of community activity. Distribution of income is not measured, so rising GDP can coexist with growing inequality that leaves most households no better off. Environmental degradation and depletion of the resource base can increase GDP in the short term, because the cost of lost resources is not deducted. These limitations show that GDP is useful for measuring market activity, but it must be supplemented by measures of distribution, sustainability and wellbeing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: several exclusions are analysed, including the effect of omitting income distribution and environmental costs, and a reasoned judgement is reached on GDP's usefulness.

sampleAnswers.answer: GDP excludes unpaid household work and the informal economy, so some valuable activity is not counted. It also ignores income distribution, so growth may not improve most households' living standards.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 5-mark response analyses two limitations with accurate evidence. Analysing environmental degradation and linking the limitations to wellbeing would move it up.

markerNotes: Reward the definition of technical recession as two consecutive quarters of negative growth

sampleAnswers.answer: Economic decline takes several forms. Negative economic growth occurs when real GDP falls over a period. A technical recession is two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth. A per capita recession occurs when real GDP per person falls, which can happen even if total GDP rises, when population grows faster than output. A depression is a severe and prolonged downturn, with very high unemployment and a large fall in output, such as the Great Depression of the 1930s.

dotPoints.description: Factors influencing the components of aggregate supply, including productivity, quality and quantity of inputs

prompts.question: Explain the factors influencing the components of aggregate supply, including productivity, quality and quantity of inputs.
markerNotes: Reward the link between productivity and output per unit of input, which shifts the aggregate supply curve to the right
Distinguishing a rise in the quantity of inputs from a rise in their quality shows precise understanding
commonStudentErrors: Confusing aggregate supply with aggregate demand
Describing inputs without explaining how they affect output
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains clearly how productivity and the quality and quantity of inputs such as labour, capital, natural resources and technology determine aggregate supply, with precise examples
5 marks: Explains the components of aggregate supply and at least two factors with accurate examples
4 marks: Explains one factor and its effect on aggregate supply with accurate detail
3 marks: Describes aggregate supply and some factors with some accuracy
2 marks: Identifies a factor affecting aggregate supply
1 mark: Makes a general statement about production

sampleAnswers.answer: Aggregate supply is the total quantity of goods and services that firms are willing to produce at a given price level, and it depends on the components of production. Productivity, the output produced per unit of input, is the most important influence, because higher productivity allows more output from the same inputs and shifts the long-run aggregate supply curve to the right. The quantity of inputs matters too: more labour, capital or natural resources allow greater output. The quality of inputs also matters, because a better-educated workforce or more advanced machinery produces more per hour. Technological change raises the quality of capital and labour together. These factors determine the economy's capacity to produce, and so its potential output.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the components of aggregate supply are explained, the effects of productivity and the quality and quantity of inputs are distinguished, and the link to potential output is identified.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aggregate supply depends on how much firms produce, and higher productivity means more output.

dotPoints.description: Relationship between actual output and potential output

prompts.question: Explain the relationship between actual output and potential output.
markerNotes: Reward the explanation that potential output is the sustainable level of production at full employment, and that exceeding it generates inflationary pressure

3 marks: Describes potential output and actual output with some accuracy

sampleAnswers.answer: Potential output is the level of production the economy can sustain at full employment without generating inflationary pressure, and actual output is the level of production in a period. When actual output is below potential output, there is a negative output gap, which indicates spare capacity, idle workers and higher unemployment. When actual output exceeds potential output, there is a positive output gap, which puts pressure on resources and tends to push up prices. The gap therefore indicates where the economy is in the business cycle. Policy makers aim to keep actual output close to potential output, because this balances employment and inflation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: both concepts are explained, the two types of output gap are distinguished, and their implications for unemployment and inflation are identified.

dotPoints.description: Construct and interpret aggregate demand and aggregate supply (AD-AS) graphs to demonstrate changes in GDP

prompts.question: Analyse, using aggregate demand and aggregate supply graphs, how changes in aggregate demand and aggregate supply affect GDP.
markerNotes: Strong answers show the new equilibrium on the graph, with the change in real GDP and in the price level identified
Reward the distinction between a shift of aggregate demand, which moves both GDP and prices in the same direction, and a shift of aggregate supply, which moves them in opposite directions
commonStudentErrors: Drawing shifts of the curves without labelling the new equilibrium

prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained analysis, supported by correctly labelled AD-AS graphs, of how shifts in aggregate demand and aggregate supply change real GDP and the price level, weighing the effects of each shift and reaching a reasoned conclusion
5-6 marks: Analyses at least one shift in aggregate demand and one in aggregate supply with accurate graphs or description
3-4 marks: Describes AD-AS shifts and their effect on GDP with some accuracy
1-2 marks: Makes a basic or general statement about aggregate demand and supply

sampleAnswers.answer: On an AD-AS graph, real GDP is shown on the horizontal axis and the price level on the vertical axis. An increase in aggregate demand, such as from higher consumer spending, shifts the AD curve to the right, raising real GDP and the price level, as the economy moves up the short-run aggregate supply curve. An increase in aggregate supply, such as from improved productivity, shifts the SRAS curve to the right, which raises real GDP and lowers the price level. A decrease in aggregate supply, such as a rise in energy costs, shifts the SRAS curve to the left, which lowers real GDP and raises the price level. The effect on GDP therefore depends on which curve shifts. An increase in aggregate demand raises both GDP and prices, while an increase in aggregate supply raises GDP and lowers prices. The graphs show that supply-side changes have different implications for policy than demand-side changes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: shifts of aggregate demand and supply are analysed with their effects on real GDP and the price level, and the difference between demand-side and supply-side changes is identified.

sampleAnswers.answer: An increase in aggregate demand shifts the AD curve to the right, which raises real GDP and the price level. A fall in aggregate supply shifts SRAS left, which lowers real GDP and raises prices.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 5-mark response analyses shifts of both curves with accurate effects. Explaining why the effects on prices differ and reaching a conclusion would move it up.

sampleAnswers.answer: When aggregate demand increases, GDP tends to increase.

sampleAnswers.answer: Economic growth raises incomes and the capacity of households to spend and save, while businesses benefit from rising demand, higher profits and the incentive to invest. Growth also raises tax revenue for the government, which can fund services and reduce welfare spending. However, the gains may be unevenly distributed, and growth can bring inflationary pressure that erodes the value of savings. Economic decline has the opposite effects. Households lose jobs and incomes, and businesses face falling sales, reduced profits and possible closure. The government receives less tax revenue while spending on welfare rises, which can widen the budget deficit. The most severe effects fall on the unemployed and low-income households, which shows that the costs and benefits of the business cycle are not shared equally.

sampleAnswers.answer: Trends in economic growth in Australia have been strong over the long term, with a long run of expansion since the early 1990s. Its main drivers have been population growth, which increases the labour force and demand, and the mining boom of the 2000s, when rising commodity prices improved the terms of trade and boosted national income and investment. Productivity growth has been slower in recent decades, which has limited growth in output per worker. Trends have also been affected by external shocks, such as the global financial crisis, which slowed growth but did not produce a recession, and the COVID-19 pandemic, which caused a sharp contraction in 2020. These trends show that growth depends on a combination of population, commodity prices and productivity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: several reasons for trends in growth are explained with precise examples, including the terms of trade and productivity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The labour force is made up of the employed and the unemployed. People who are neither employed nor unemployed, such as students or retirees not seeking work, are outside the labour force, so they are not counted in the unemployment rate.

sampleAnswers.answer: Labour force participation is the proportion of the working-age population that is in the labour force. Cyclical influences change with the business cycle: in an economic downturn, some people become discouraged and leave the labour force, lowering participation, while recovery draws them back. Structural influences change more slowly. The ageing population means a growing share of people are beyond typical working age, which lowers participation, while rising female participation over several decades has raised it. Changes in education, retirement patterns and the flexibility of work arrangements also affect participation. Understanding both types of influence helps policy makers distinguish temporary changes from long-term trends.

sampleAnswers.answer: Demographic shifts, particularly an ageing population, raise Australia's dependency ratio, which is the number of dependants relative to the working-age population. This affects economic growth because a smaller share of the population is in the workforce, which slows labour force growth and can reduce output per person unless productivity rises. Government revenue is also affected, as fewer workers pay income tax, while spending on pensions, aged care and health rises, which can widen the budget deficit. Policy responses include increasing immigration, which adds workers and taxpayers, and raising the retirement age, which keeps people in the labour force for longer. However, immigration may raise infrastructure and social pressures and its benefits depend on the skills of migrants, while raising the retirement age may be unpopular and affects those in physically demanding jobs. The implications are therefore serious for the budget and growth, and policy must combine workforce participation, productivity and migration.

sampleAnswers.answer: The causes of unemployment are several. Insufficient aggregate demand occurs when spending falls and firms cut jobs to reduce costs, as in a recession. Structural changes, such as the decline of manufacturing, leave workers with skills that are no longer demanded. Technological change can replace routine tasks, so some jobs disappear while others require new skills. Labour market frictions, such as the time taken to find work and imperfect information about vacancies, cause unemployment even when jobs exist. Underemployment, where people work fewer hours than they want, is often caused by insufficient demand and by the growth of part-time and casual work, so workers are employed but not fully utilised.

dotPoints.description: Limitations of measuring the rate of unemployment, including hidden unemployed, underemployed and informal workers

prompts.question: Analyse the limitations of measuring the rate of unemployment, including hidden unemployed, underemployed and informal workers.
markerNotes: Strong answers explain that the unemployment rate excludes people who have given up looking, understating the labour market's slack

sampleAnswers.answer: The unemployment rate is a widely used measure of labour market slack, but it has important limitations. It excludes hidden unemployed people, who want work but have stopped looking because they believe no jobs are available, so the rate understates the true lack of work, especially in downturns. Underemployed workers, who want more hours, are counted as employed, so the rate does not reflect those who cannot get enough work. Informal workers, who are paid without formal records, may be missed by surveys, which underestimates the scale of insecure employment. These limitations matter for policy. If policymakers rely on the rate alone, they may judge the labour market to be healthier than it is and may withdraw stimulus too early. The analysis suggests the rate should be read alongside measures of underemployment and participation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the limitations are analysed with their effect on the measure, the implications for policy are explained, and a reasoned conclusion is reached.

sampleAnswers.answer: The unemployment rate excludes hidden unemployed people who have stopped looking for work. Underemployed workers are counted as employed, so the rate does not show their lack of hours.

sampleAnswers.answer: A budget deficit can be financed in three ways, each with limitations. Debt financing, through borrowing from financial markets, creates servicing costs in the form of interest payments, which rise with the level of debt and reduce funds for other spending. Monetary financing, where the central bank creates money to fund government spending, avoids servicing costs, but increases the money supply and risks inflation, which erodes the real value of incomes and savings. Asset sales raise revenue once, but they lose the future income the assets would have generated, and they may be unpopular. Each method therefore trades a short-term benefit against a cost that falls on future budgets or on the price level, so the choice depends on the economic circumstances and on the sustainability of the debt.

sampleAnswers.answer: The effectiveness of fiscal policy in achieving Australia's economic objectives can be evaluated, using relevant data, against whether it stabilised the economy, supported employment, controlled inflation and reduced inequality. During the global financial crisis, a discretionary stimulus and automatic stabilisers helped Australia avoid recession, and growth continued, which suggests that fiscal policy was effective in stabilising demand. sampleAnswers.answer: Absolute advantage exists when a country can produce a good with fewer resources than another country. Comparative advantage exists when a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost, meaning it gives up less of other goods to produce it. For example, if Australia can produce 10 tonnes of wheat or 2 tonnes of steel with a given set of resources, and another country can produce 5 tonnes of wheat or 1 tonne of steel, Australia has an absolute advantage in both, but its opportunity cost of steel is 5 tonnes of wheat compared with the other country's 5 tonnes for steel too, so the comparison depends on the ratios. The principle shows that trade benefits both countries when each specialises in the good for which it has the lower opportunity cost, even if one country has an absolute advantage in both goods.

markerNotes: Reward the explanation that the Australian dollar rose during the commodity boom of the 2000s and fell as commodity prices declined

commonStudentErrors: Describing trends without naming the factors
Attributing all movements to domestic interest rates
keywords: trends in the value of the Australian dollar
prompts.markingCriteria:

sampleAnswers.answer: The trends in the value of the Australian dollar reflect the commodity price cycle, and its major trends have reasons linked to commodity prices. It rose strongly during the mining boom of the 2000s, when high prices for iron ore and coal increased export income and demand for the dollar. It fell as commodity prices declined after 2011, and it fell sharply during the global financial crisis as investors moved to safer assets. Interest rate differentials have also mattered: higher Australian interest rates relative to other economies have supported the dollar, while rate cuts have weighed on it. These trends show that the dollar is closely linked to commodity prices, global risk sentiment and the relative stance of monetary policy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: major trends are explained with the commodity cycle, global risk sentiment and interest rate differentials, with dated examples.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Australian dollar rose during the mining boom because commodity prices were high.

sampleAnswers.answer: Economic development is a broader concept than economic growth, and it has several features. Economic structure refers to the shift of production from agriculture towards manufacturing and services, which typically raises productivity and incomes. Education raises human capital, which improves productivity and opportunities. Health outcomes, such as life expectancy and infant mortality, reflect and support development. Sustainability requires that development does not deplete the resource base or damage the environment for future generations. Countries that improve these features together tend to achieve more inclusive and lasting development.

sampleAnswers.answer: Economic development includes changes in the structure of the economy and improvements in education.

sampleAnswers.answer: The relationship between economic growth and economic development is that growth, an increase in output over time, is usually necessary for economic development, because higher incomes allow investment in education, health and infrastructure. However, growth is not sufficient. If its benefits are concentrated among a small group, or if it depletes the resource base, development may stall and wellbeing may not improve. Inclusive growth spreads benefits across the population, and sustainable growth protects the environment, which supports long-term wellbeing. Some economies have grown rapidly while leaving large groups in poverty, while others have achieved strong development outcomes with more modest growth through investment in health and education. The importance of inclusive and sustainable growth lies in ensuring that growth translates into lasting improvements in living standards.

prompts.question: Describe the measures of economic development, including the Human Development Index (HDI), GDP adjusted for a common currency, differences in population and purchasing power parity (PPP).
markerNotes: Reward the explanation that the HDI combines income, education and health, and that PPP adjusts GDP for differences in price levels across countries

commonStudentErrors: Describing the HDI as a measure of income only

sampleAnswers.answer: The measures of economic development include the Human Development Index, which combines life expectancy, education and income into a single measure, so it captures wellbeing beyond income. Purchasing power parity adjusts GDP for differences in prices between countries, so that incomes can be compared by what they can buy. GDP per person, adjusted to a common currency, gives a measure of average income, but it must be adjusted for population differences, since countries of different sizes produce different totals. Each measure has limits: the HDI does not capture inequality within a country, and GDP per capita omits distribution and non-market activity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The characteristics of least developed countries include very low incomes, high levels of poverty, weak institutions and limited infrastructure, and a dependence on agriculture. Developing countries have low to middle incomes and are industrialising, but face gaps in health, education and infrastructure. Emerging economies are developing countries that have grown rapidly, become integrated into global markets and developed manufacturing or financial sectors, such as China and India. Advanced economies have high incomes, service-based structures, strong institutions and high living standards, such as Australia and Japan.

prompts.question: Analyse the factors contributing to differences in economic development between countries, including the strength of institutions, geography and natural resource endowment, quality of human capital and infrastructure.
markerNotes: Strong answers show that natural resource wealth can weaken institutions, through corruption or dependence on a single export, rather than always helping development

Describing geography as determining development without explaining the mechanism

7-8 marks: Makes a sustained analysis of the factors contributing to differences in economic development between countries, weighing institutions, geography, resources, human capital and infrastructure, and showing how they interact, with a reasoned conclusion

3-4 marks: Describes factors contributing to differences in development with some accuracy

sampleAnswers.answer: Differences in economic development between countries arise from institutions, geography, resources, human capital and infrastructure, and these factors interact. The strength of institutions, such as secure property rights, an independent judiciary and low corruption, encourages investment and innovation, and they are often considered the most important factor. Geography affects development through climate, access to the sea and disease burdens, which can raise costs and limit agriculture. Natural resource endowment can help development, but it can also weaken institutions when governments depend on resource rents, a pattern known as the resource curse. Human capital, shaped by education and health, determines productivity, while infrastructure, such as transport and power, lowers the cost of doing business. The factors reinforce one another: good institutions can improve human capital and infrastructure, while poor institutions can trap countries in low development. The conclusion is that institutions are central, but they operate through the other factors.

sampleAnswers.answer: Climate change raises global equity issues because the uneven distribution of its economic costs is stark, while the countries most affected have contributed least to the emissions that cause it. Low-income and tropical countries face greater exposure to drought, flooding and rising sea levels, and they have fewer resources to adapt, so their agriculture, infrastructure and health systems suffer more. Wealthy countries, which have historically produced most emissions, can more readily afford adaptation and insurance. This mismatch between responsibility and burden raises questions about fairness and compensation. International responses, such as climate finance commitments and the loss and damage fund agreed at the 2022 climate conference, aim to address these issues, although the scale of funding remains debated. The conclusion is that global equity requires that responsibility for emissions be linked to support for adaptation.

sampleAnswers.answer: International economic development has substantially reduced absolute poverty over recent decades, with the share of the world's population living on extreme poverty falling sharply, largely because of rapid growth in China and other parts of East Asia. This reduction reflects growth, trade and the spread of technology, along with international aid and public health improvements. However, the effects have been uneven. The geographical distribution of extreme poverty has shifted, so that a larger share of the remaining poor now live in sub-Saharan Africa and in fragile or conflict-affected states, where growth has been slower and institutions weaker. Those regions face high population growth and vulnerability to climate shocks. The assessment is that international development in the global economy has greatly reduced the level of absolute poverty, but its benefits have not reached all regions, and the remaining poverty is more concentrated and harder to reduce.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Australian economy is vulnerable to fluctuations in regional and international business cycles for several reasons. Its exports are concentrated in commodities, such as iron ore and coal, so a slowdown in demand from major trading partners, particularly China, reduces export prices and income. Trade dependence means that a downturn in the global economy quickly affects output and employment. Australia also relies on foreign capital inflows to finance its current account deficit, so a withdrawal of investment in a global downturn can raise borrowing costs and depreciate the exchange rate, which in turn raises import prices. Its exchange rate can move sharply with commodity prices and global risk sentiment, adding volatility. The analysis shows that the economy's vulnerability comes from the interaction of commodity concentration, trade dependence and reliance on capital, which transmit regional and global cycles into domestic conditions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: several factors are analysed, their links to regional and global business cycles are shown, and a reasoned conclusion is drawn about the interaction of the factors.

sampleAnswers.answer: Several factors have contributed to the resilience of the Australian economy against external shocks. A floating exchange rate allows the dollar to depreciate when the economy is hit by a shock, which cushions the effect on exports and absorbs the adjustment without requiring large falls in domestic wages and employment. Flexible monetary policy, with an independent central bank that can lower interest rates, provides a tool to support demand. Strong institutions, including a sound banking system and prudent financial regulation, reduced the impact of the global financial crisis. The economy's diverse and growing services sector also reduces dependence on any single industry. Together these factors allowed Australia to avoid recession during the global financial crisis.

sampleAnswers.answer: Changes in the global economy affect both the performance and the structure of Australia's economy. In performance terms, a stronger global economy raises demand for Australian exports, supporting growth and employment, while a global downturn reduces export income and can slow growth. Changes in global commodity prices affect the terms of trade, income and the exchange rate, which in turn affect inflation through import prices. In structural terms, global competition and technological change have contributed to the decline of manufacturing and the growth of services, including education and tourism, which now earn substantial export income. Globalisation has also shifted investment and production across borders, changing the mix of industries and regions. The overall effect is that Australia's performance has become more sensitive to global conditions, and its structure has moved towards sectors that are linked to global demand.
